title: Given an integer array, return an array where each position holds the product of all other elements, without using division and in linear time.
shortTitle: Product of Array Except Self — Prefix Product Times Suffix Product

s1_definition.profdef: Product of array except self computes, for each index, the product of everything to its left times the product of everything to its right, avoiding division. Using two sweeps, a left-to-right prefix-product pass and a right-to-left suffix-product pass accumulated into the same output array, it runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra space beyond the output.
s1_definition.analogy: The bank has a row of daily growth factors and wants, for each day, the combined growth of all the other days. Instead of dividing the total by that day, which breaks if any day is zero, the clerk makes one left-to-right pass writing the running product of earlier days, then one right-to-left pass multiplying in the running product of later days. Each position ends up holding everything except itself.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fill each slot with the product of everything on its left, then multiply in the product of everything on its right.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Product of array except self computes, for each index, the product of everything to its left times the product of everything to its right, avoiding division. Using two sweeps, a left-to-right prefix-product pass and a right-to-left suffix-product pass accumulated into the same output array, it runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra space beyond the output.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The bank has a row of daily growth factors and wants, for each day, the combined growth of all the other days. Instead of dividing the total by that day, which breaks if any day is zero, the clerk makes one left-to-right pass writing the running product of earlier days, then one right-to-left pass multiplying in the running product of later days. Each position ends up holding everything except itself.

**One line to remember:** Fill each slot with the product of everything on its left, then multiply in the product of everything on its right.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive approach multiplies all elements and divides by each, but the problem forbids division, and division also fails if any element is zero. The prefix-suffix approach sidesteps both issues.

The result at index i is the product of all elements left of i times the product of all elements right of i. We compute this in two passes using the output array itself to hold intermediate products, so we use no extra array.

First pass, left to right: `result[0] = 1; for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) result[i] = result[i - 1] * nums[i - 1];`. After this, result[i] holds the product of everything strictly to the left of i.

Second pass, right to left, using a running suffix variable: `int suffix = 1; for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) { result[i] *= suffix; suffix *= nums[i]; }`. Here suffix accumulates the product of everything to the right of i, and we multiply it into the already-stored left product.

The output array holds the final answer, and the only extra variable is the suffix scalar, so extra space is O(1) if the output array is not counted, which is the standard convention.

A senior-level nuance is zero handling, which this method handles for free. If one element is zero, every other position correctly gets zero multiplied somewhere, and the zero position gets the product of all non-zero neighbors, all without any special casing, whereas the division approach would divide by zero or need branching.

Another nuance for money is that true monetary products are rare, but growth factors, interest multipliers, and risk weights are multiplied, and those should use BigDecimal to stay exact; the algorithm is identical with multiply in place of the primitive star.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India tracks a sequence of daily growth multipliers for a portfolio and wants, for each day, the combined growth contributed by all the other days, to measure each day's isolation effect. Using total-divided-by-day is unsafe because a flat day with a multiplier that could be zero in a stress scenario would cause a division error. This is exactly the product-of-array-except-self problem.

Problem 2 — The computation must be linear over long histories, so we use the two-pass prefix-and-suffix method rather than recomputing each position's product from scratch, which would be quadratic.

Problem 3 — We avoid division entirely, which also means the method is robust to a zero multiplier without any special handling.

In the code: a `ProductAnalyzer` has a `productExceptSelf` method using the two-pass technique. An `ExceptSelfDemo` main computes the result for a sample growth array including a case that shows zero-safety conceptually with integers.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: growth 2, 3, 4, 5 (indices 0 to 3). Expected output is 60, 40, 30, 24, because for index 0 it is 3 times 4 times 5, and so on.

Pass 1 (left products): result[0] is 1. result[1] is result[0] times nums[0], 1 times 2 equals 2. result[2] is result[1] times nums[1], 2 times 3 equals 6. result[3] is result[2] times nums[2], 6 times 4 equals 24. Now result holds 1, 2, 6, 24, which are the products of everything to the left of each index.

Pass 2 (suffix products): suffix starts at 1. At index 3, result[3] times suffix is 24 times 1 equals 24, then suffix becomes 1 times nums[3] equals 5. At index 2, result[2] times suffix is 6 times 5 equals 30, suffix becomes 5 times 4 equals 20. At index 1, result[1] times suffix is 2 times 20 equals 40, suffix becomes 20 times 3 equals 60. At index 0, result[0] times suffix is 1 times 60 equals 60.

Final result is 60, 40, 30, 24.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26 23:20:00 [INFO] Computing product of all other days for each day (no division)
2026-10-26 23:20:00 [INFO] Input  -> [2, 3, 4, 5]
2026-10-26 23:20:00 [INFO] Result -> [60, 40, 30, 24]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [2 3 4 5]
    │
    ▼ Pass 1 left→right (left products into result)
  result = [1 2 6 24]
    │
    ▼ Pass 2 right→left (multiply running suffix)
  i3: 24*1=24  suffix=5
  i2: 6*5 =30  suffix=20
  i1: 2*20=40  suffix=60
  i0: 1*60=60
    │
    ▼
  Output: [60 40 30 24]   (no division, zero-safe)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Product of array except self asks for, at each position, the product of every other element, and the twist is that I must do it without division and in linear time. I cannot just compute the total product and divide it out per element, both because the problem forbids division and because division breaks the moment any element is zero. The clean solution is two sweeps. In the first sweep, left to right, I fill each output slot with the product of everything strictly to its left. In the second sweep, right to left, I carry a running suffix product and multiply it into each slot, so each position ends up holding its left product times its right product, which is exactly the product of everything except itself.

The elegant part is the space usage. I reuse the output array to hold the left-product intermediates during the first pass, and the only extra storage in the second pass is a single scalar for the running suffix, so beyond the required output array I use constant extra space.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this to compute, for each day in a portfolio's sequence of daily growth multipliers, the combined growth contributed by all the other days, which measures each day's isolation effect. Dividing the overall product by a single day would be unsafe because a stress-scenario flat day could carry a zero multiplier and blow up the division, whereas this two-pass method handles a zero naturally with no special casing at all.

I also point out that for genuine financial products like compounded interest multipliers or risk weights I would hold the values in BigDecimal and use its multiply method to stay exact, and the algorithm is structurally identical. The key interview insight is recognizing that a left-product array and a right-product sweep together reconstruct the except-self product, which is the same precompute-and-combine thinking behind prefix sums applied to multiplication.
